e.t: This word describes someone as “not competent” or “unworthy”—not fit or deserving for a matter under consideration. It expresses an assessment of a person’s suitability or worthiness, rather than naming an action itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 6:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a negative judgment about being qualified or worthy.

This word describes a straightforward, sincere way of being—without divided motives, complication, or pretense. It can refer to the purity of a person’s conduct, intentions, or devotion. In English Bible renderings, it is expressed as “simplicity” and “sincerity,” which together point to an undivided and genuine character. The word occurs eight times in the Greek New Testament, including passages in Romans, 2 Corinthians, Ephesians, and Colossians.

This word refers to a hill known as Mars’ Hill, or to the meeting of the Areopagus. It functions as a place-name rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in two verses in Acts 17. The wording can emphasize the physical hill itself or the associated meeting place, so the surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent. Its central meaning remains the named location connected with the Areopagus.

This word means “plow,” the farm tool used to break and prepare soil for planting. It is a noun naming an agricultural implement rather than an action or a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 9:62. Its ordinary meaning is straightforward, while the significance of its use in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage. [p03:word:greek-nt:G0723:identity, p03:word:greek-nt:G0723:occurrences]

Foolishness means foolish thinking or behavior—acting without sound judgment or wisdom. In the Greek New Testament, the word appears four times: once in Mark and three times in 2 Corinthians. It names a quality rather than a person, describing what is foolish in thought or conduct. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Bartholomew is a personal name identifying a specific person in the Greek New Testament. It is not presented as a general quality, action, or description, but as the name by which this individual is identified. The name occurs four times in the New Testament: in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Acts. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “harmful,” describing something that causes damage, injury, or loss rather than benefit. It identifies a damaging quality or effect and is used as a description, not as the name of a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 6:9. The surrounding verse supplies the specific situation in which this harmful quality is being discussed.

This word means “treasury,” referring to a place or repository for money. It is a noun used for the location associated with collected or stored funds. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times across four verses, all rendered “treasury.” Its references occur in Mark, Luke, and John, showing that the word names a recognized treasury rather than describing a person or an action. The precise significance of the treasury in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “thirst,” referring to the physical desire or need for water. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:27. Its basic meaning is straightforward: it describes experiencing thirst rather than offering a symbolic definition by itself. The surrounding verse determines how that experience contributes to the sentence, but the word’s ordinary sense remains the bodily condition of needing or longing for drink.

This word means “governor,” referring to a person who exercises authority over a people or territory. It describes an official ruler rather than a general idea of leadership. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:32. The word’s basic sense identifies the governing authority involved; the surrounding verse is needed to understand the particular situation in which that governor appears.

This word means “if” and introduces a condition: it presents something as dependent on another possibility or circumstance. In New Testament sentences, it helps connect what may happen, what is assumed, or what follows from a stated situation. It is a connecting word rather than a name for a person, object, or action. It occurs 65 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing across 29 verses. Its exact force in any passage depends on the words and argument surrounding it.

e.t: This word describes being deeply agitated or giving a stern warning. It can express strong inner disturbance, and it can also describe an urgent, serious admonition directed toward someone else. Thus, its central idea is not mild concern but an intense reaction or forceful warning. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages in Matthew, Mark, and John. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis falls on emotional agitation or on warning someone firmly.

e.t: This word means “be present” or “the present,” referring to what is currently here or occurring rather than what is past or future. It can describe a present time, circumstance, or condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, commonly rendered “present,” and its sense remains centered on what is at hand. The surrounding sentence determines whether it points to people, events, or circumstances that are presently involved or taking place.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to search intently” or “to search out.” It describes careful, purposeful investigation rather than a casual glance or passing interest. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Peter 1:10, so its normal meaning is established from that single occurrence and its explicit lexical definitions. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the action being described there.

This Greek New Testament word means “coming” or “oversight,” referring either to an arrival or to watchful responsibility, depending on how it functions in a sentence. These two meanings share the idea of attention directed toward someone or something: one may look toward a coming event, or take responsibility by watching over others. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing once each in Luke, Acts, 1 Timothy, and 1 Peter.

e.t: This word means “at once” or “once for all,” emphasizing a single occurrence rather than something repeated. In the Greek New Testament, it is used five times. Its meaning can describe an action that happens one time, or an act whose lasting significance means it does not need to be repeated. The surrounding sentence determines which emphasis is strongest. It appears especially in Hebrews, where the word helps express the completeness and finality of an act performed once for all.

Zerah is a personal name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears once, in Matthew 1:3, and is rendered “Zerah.” Because it is a proper name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it distinguishes this individual from the other people named in the surrounding genealogy. The name itself does not function as a description or command; understanding its particular significance depends on the larger biblical context concerning the person named.

This word means “Thessalonica,” the name of a place mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea. The word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, in Acts, Philippians, and 2 Timothy. Its references connect it with the setting of Paul’s ministry and with believers’ support and travel, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each specific occurrence.

This word means “horse” or “horses,” referring to the animal. It is a noun used for horses generally, whether one animal or more than one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 17 times, appearing once in James and frequently in Revelation. Its basic meaning remains the same in each occurrence; the surrounding passage determines what the horses are doing or how they relate to the scene. The word first appears in James 3:3 and continues through Revelation 19:21.

e.t: This Greek verb means “to be pierced” or “to pierce.” It describes the act of piercing, whether the emphasis rests on something receiving the piercing or on someone carrying it out. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 2:37. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains piercing—an action expressed either as received or performed.

e.t: This word means “to be filled to the full” or “to satisfy.” It describes reaching a state in which a need or desire has been fully met, or causing that fullness in someone else. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so its basic meaning is clear even though its precise force in each verse depends on the surrounding context. It appears in Acts 27:38 and 1 Corinthians 4:8. The word can therefore point either to being completely filled or to satisfying another.

This word means “southwest,” referring to a direction or wind coming from the southwest. It is a geographical term that identifies where something comes from or toward which it moves. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:12. The word itself names the southwest direction; its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and voyage description, which are handled separately. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: the southwest.

Matthias is a personal name—the name of the man chosen to take Judas’s place among the apostles. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears twice, both times in Acts 1:23 and Acts 1:26. The word itself identifies the person rather than describing a quality, action, or spiritual concept. Its precise significance in those verses depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is simply the name Matthias.

e.t: This word means “to remember” or “remembering”—to bring something back to mind and keep it in mind. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 21 times as an expression concerning recollection. It can describe recalling what Jesus or others previously said, remembering past events, or keeping a person’s words before one’s mind. Its ordinary sense is active remembrance rather than merely possessing information. The surrounding sentence determines what is being recalled and why it matters.

This word refers to a chick or young bird. Its basic meaning is the small offspring of a bird, expressed by the glosses “chick” and “chicks.” It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 13:34. The word itself identifies the young bird; the surrounding verse determines how that image functions in its immediate context. No broader meaning is required by the word’s lexical sense.

e.t: This word means “eight,” the number that follows seven and comes before nine. It identifies a quantity or count in the Greek New Testament, rather than expressing an action, quality, or personal name. It occurs eight times across eight verses, appearing in Luke, John, Acts, and 1 Peter. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it is used; the surrounding verse determines what people, things, or days are being counted. [p03:word:greek-nt:G3638:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G3638:occurrences]

This Greek New Testament word describes something as “straight” or “upright,” conveying the idea of being properly aligned rather than bent or out of line. It occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Acts and once in Hebrews. Both major English renderings preserve the same central idea, using “upright” in one place and “straight” in the other. The precise force in either verse depends on its surrounding context.

This word describes people who have been brought in secretly or have infiltrated a group. It points to an unnoticed or concealed entrance, emphasizing that those involved were not openly introduced. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Galatians 2:4. The word’s central idea is hidden entry: someone has gained access without being recognized or accepted openly. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the people being described.

This word means “more than” or “superabundant,” describing something that exceeds an expected amount, degree, or comparison. It can point to an additional measure, a greater extent, or an abundance beyond what is ordinary. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times across 15 verses, so its basic sense is used in several kinds of statements rather than being limited to one subject. The surrounding words determine what is greater or more abundant in a particular verse.

e.t: This word means “to increase,” “to grow,” or “to become more.” It describes something becoming greater in amount, extent, or effect, and it can also express causing something to increase. In the Greek New Testament, it is used nine times across eight verses. Its wording can describe increase as something that happens or as something brought about by another person or circumstance. The surrounding sentence determines what is increasing and whether the word is stating an actual increase, expressing a possible increase, or describing an intended result.

This word means “of what kind?” It is used to ask about the nature, character, or sort of something rather than merely identifying it. Depending on the sentence, it can express wonder, questioning, or a request to recognize what something is like. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times, appearing in questions or statements that draw attention to the kind or quality of a person or thing. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is asking or pointing out what kind something is.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to nail” or “to nail to.” It describes the action of fastening something by driving nails into it. The word focuses on the act of attachment rather than on the object being fastened or the result afterward. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Colossians 2:14, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated passages.

e.h: Asking How or In What Way
e.t: This word asks “how?”—that is, “in what way?” It is used to ask about the manner, means, or possibility of something. In some settings, it can express uncertainty with the sense “perhaps” or “somehow,” depending on the sentence. It appears 118 times in the Greek New Testament, so it is a common question word rather than a term limited to one subject or situation. Its exact force in a particular verse comes from the surrounding words and sentence.

This word means “sandals,” referring to simple footwear worn on the feet. It is a plural noun naming an item of clothing rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, appearing once in Mark and once in Acts. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: sandals, or footwear made to be worn on the feet. The surrounding verse determines what instruction or event involving the sandals is intended.

e.t: This word means “to settle” or “to settle accounts.” It describes bringing an account or obligation to a clear reckoning and resolution rather than leaving it unresolved. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Matthew. Its central idea is the completion of an accounting or settlement. The surrounding passage determines the particular force in each occurrence, but the word consistently points to dealing with an account until it is settled.

This word means a bond or bondage: something that binds, holds together, or places someone under restraint. It can describe a connecting bond between people or things, as well as a condition of being bound. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, including uses rendered “bond.” Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This verb means “to mature,” describing something that reaches full development or becomes fully formed. It presents maturity as a completed result rather than merely beginning to grow. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 8:14; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the way the sentence is constructed. The word therefore points to reaching the intended stage of development, not simply existing or making progress toward it.

This verb means “to experience” or “to undergo”—to pass through something and be affected by it. It describes what happens to a person or group as they encounter a particular condition, event, or consequence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Jude 1:7, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense focuses on personally passing through or enduring something, rather than merely observing it from a distance.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “yesterday,” referring to the day immediately before the present day or the day being discussed. It identifies a past time in relation to the speaker’s or writer’s current point of reference. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, in John 4:52, Acts 7:28, and Hebrews 13:8. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: it points to the preceding day, while the surrounding verse determines why that past time is mentioned.
